newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Peters says low confidence hits NZ fiscal outlook.
newsitem.headline: Peters says low confidence hits NZ fiscal outlook.

text.p: New Zealand's Treasurer and Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters, just three weeks away from his first budget, admitted on Thursday that low business confidence meant 1997/98 growth forecasts had to be cut.

Though he gave no specific details, he said the coalition government believed the GDP growth rate had bottomed at above 2.0 percent in the current cycle, a level well below that predicted six months ago when the coalition was formed.

"The lower business confidence means that Treasury's (growth) forecasts for the coming year will be revised down and that has a significant effect on tax (income)," he told a business audience in a lunchtime address.

However, in an unusually clear affirmation that the economic policy aims of his New Zealand First party remained intact, Peters insisted that after going ahead with promised hikes in public spending the overall budget would remain in surplus.
"Even after taking into account lower business confidence we will continue running surpluses," he promised, in the speech to the Marlborough Chamber of Commerce.

The broad outlines for the budget have been clear since March, when the centre-right coalition of NZ First and the conservative National Party made a budget policy statement with NZ$5.0 billion (nearly $3.5 billion) of extra spending on health and education over the next three years at its core.

In tandem, the new incumbents predicted a "soft landing" for the economy during the current year that would soon see an upswing in activity to ensure healthy fiscal surpluses and create room for over NZ$1.0 billion in tax cuts next year.
In his speech on Thursday Peters indicated that expected surplus rates would now have to be revised downwards in the budget.

"Markets and commentators shouldn't expect the same track of surpluses described in the budget policy statement. We're sticking faithfully to our expenditure policy targets, but it is clear that tax flows won't be as strong," Peters warned.
It was a message that came as no surprise to most market analysts, as many have interpreted recent data from the real economy as showing no indication of a rapid upturn.
But political opponents of the coalition, and New Zealand First in particular, pounced on the speech to challenge the coalition's approach to economic management.
Some went as far as to blame Peters -- back in the media firing line on Thursday over a cash-for-interviews row involving one of his MPs -- for being part of the confidence crisis.
Free market party Act New Zealand's economics spokesman Rodney Hide said New Zealand First should dump the errant MP Tukoroirangi Morgan as it would boost the economy.
"We are in a politically-induced recession," Hide told Reuters.

His comments were echoed by the main opposition Labour Party's deputy leader, Michael Cullen, who noted that at the same time as Morgan made "true confessions" on his attempts to get paid for media interviews, Peters had come clean on the economy.
"Following hard on Morgan's recovered memory syndrome, Peters has had to admit that the deteriorating economy is having a significant fiscal impact," Cullen said.
He said the disclosure should serve to remind New Zealanders that tax cuts remained only a promise, and that the uncertainty of the economic outlook meant they could not be guaranteed.
Peters, by contrast, said businesses had to consider the impact of weak confidence as their decisions were "a crucial aspect of how the New Zealand economy performs" at this stage.
"At the end of the day it's your decisions, on whether or not to take on staff, or whether or not to go ahead with a new investment, that make the difference," he said.
